source_title: The More You Buy, The More You Lose
other_side: Zitron's answer to "which model fits your stack" is that the question is downstream of an economics problem no release solves. In The More You Buy, The More You Lose he argues the build-out is a cost spiral — borrowing to buy GPUs inflates the price of memory, power and construction, which raises the debt, which raises the payoff required — and he takes the same NVIDIA backstop this edition reports as his central exhibit, reading a $250bn guarantee for a SoftBank-affiliate site as circular financing nested inside circular financing, with Lucent and Winstar as the precedent. He never mentions Opus 5, Anthropic's models or benchmarks at all; his claim is that outside coding these systems have, in his words, "no fundamental use cases", and that the per-token prices any procurement decision is judged at are subsidised rather than real. On the enterprise side he is harsher still, quoting consultant Nik Suresh's observation of "0% success in a year and a half" across the AI projects his team watched, and describing adoption driven by executives who have never used the tools.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether better models convert into money somebody keeps paying. Both accept the frontier is jagged: NLW's own guests call Opus 5 brilliant in flashes and frustrating in practice, and Zitron's case depends on that unevenness being the norm rather than the exception. The empirical question that will resolve is whether inference at real effort settings clears a margin once discounts end, and the observable is disclosed gross margins and full-price renewal rates at Anthropic and OpenAI. The residue is worldview: whether ecosystem lock-in is a rational architecture decision or, as Zitron reads it, procurement theatre. NLW is vindicated if locked-in enterprises upgrade and stay at unsubsidised prices; Zitron if the spending is sustained only by vendor guarantees and the seats quietly lapse. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW's show needs launches to matter, Zitron's subscriptions need collapse to be certain. Where they agree is the signal: both now think benchmark scores have stopped tracking usefulness. Watch the NVIDIA backstop terms.
